events.title: The Council of Ephesus proclaims Mary Mother of God
events.shortBlurb: The third ecumenical council condemned Nestorius and confessed the Virgin Mary as Theotokos, the God-bearer…
body: Nestorius, made Patriarch of Constantinople in 428, unsettled the Church by preaching that the Virgin Mary should be called Christotokos, 'Mother of Christ,' rather than Theotokos, 'Mother of God.' Cyril of Alexandria answered him, Celestine I condemned his teaching at a Roman synod in 430, and the emperor Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus.

On 22 June 431, before the Eastern bishops and the Roman legates had arrived, Cyril opened the council with some two hundred bishops in the church of St. Mary. Nestorius, thrice summoned, refused to appear; that same day the fathers examined his writings, condemned his doctrine, and deposed him from his see.

John of Antioch, arriving late, held a rival assembly and deposed Cyril in turn, but the emperor at length confirmed the council's sentence, and Nestorius died in exile in Egypt about 451. The faith of Ephesus — one Christ, true God and true man, whose mother is therefore truly Mother of God — remains the ground of Catholic devotion to Our Lady.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. John Fisher
events.shortBlurb: The Bishop of Rochester was beheaded for refusing to acknowledge Henry VIII as head of the Church in England…
body: John Fisher, born at Beverley in Yorkshire in 1469, rose from Michaelhouse, Cambridge, to be chancellor of that university and, in 1504, Bishop of Rochester. A scholar and preacher of European fame, he defended the marriage of Queen Catherine and, alone among the English bishops, refused the oath acknowledging Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church.

Imprisoned in the Tower in April 1534, he was created cardinal by Paul III in May 1535, it is said in hope of protecting him; Henry is reported to have answered that the pope might send Fisher a hat, but he should have no head to set it on. Tried at Westminster on 17 June, he was condemned for treason.

On 22 June 1535 he was beheaded on Tower Hill, declaring that he died for the faith of Christ's holy Catholic Church. His friend Thomas More followed him a fortnight later, and Pius XI canonized the two together in 1935.

events.title: The abjuration of Galileo
events.shortBlurb: Galileo Galilei was made to renounce the Copernican doctrine before the Roman Inquisition…
body: Galileo Galilei, born at Pisa in 1564, had been admonished in 1616 not to hold or teach the Copernican doctrine of the earth's motion. When his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appeared in 1632, he was summoned to Rome and tried by the Roman Inquisition.

On 22 June 1633, in the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, the aging philosopher knelt and abjured the doctrine as contrary to Scripture. Judged 'vehemently suspected of heresy,' he was sentenced to formal imprisonment, at once commuted — first briefly to the Tuscan embassy at the Villa Medici, then to the house of the Archbishop of Siena, and at last to his own villa at Arcetri near Florence, where he died in 1642.

The sentence made Galileo's name a byword for the supposed warfare of faith and science. On 31 October 1992 John Paul II, closing the work of a commission he had appointed, acknowledged the errors of his judges and called the affair a tragic misunderstanding.
